F1.quote: he mentions the "Crimson Hexagon", which has its own meaning as an almost soul-consuming wish
F1.claim: the asker: the Crimson Hexagon as an almost soul-consuming wish
F1.lineage: the room as wish and goal

F2.quote: so much of this short story is analogous to and symbolism for real-world objects. So, what does the "crimson hexagon" represent?
F2.claim: the asker: the story is analogous to and symbolism for real-world objects; what does the hexagon represent
F2.lineage: the question of what the room represents

F3.quote: A central concern of The Library of Babel — and particularly this section of it — is the search for order and meaning within a chaotic world.
F3.claim: the story's (and the passage's) central concern: the search for order and meaning in a chaotic world
F3.lineage: the search for order and meaning

F4.quote: So, the Purifiers are a form of destructive, narrow-minded zealotry.
F4.claim: the Purifiers as destructive, narrow-minded zealotry

F5.quote: The Crimson Hexagon, mentioned so briefly, is given as the object the Purifiers are seeking.
F5.claim: the Crimson Hexagon, mentioned briefly, as the object the Purifiers seek
F5.lineage: the room in the Purifiers passage

F6.quote: the Crimson Hexagon is imagined as an utter exception to that, breaking every single rule of the world as we understand it
F6.claim: the room as an utter exception to the Library's constant structure

F7.quote: what the Purifiers, the zealots, are seeking is the impossible
F7.lineage: the room as wish and goal

F8.quote: it seems extremely doubtful that any will ever find it
F8.claim: doubtful that any will find it
F8.lineage: the room as wish and goal

F9.quote: if the Crimson Hexagon is indeed their object, their own methods are a waste of time: the Crimson Hexagon would be easily identifiable
F9.claim: the Purifiers' method is a waste of time: the room would be easily identifiable

F10.quote: This Crimson Hexagon also stands in contrast to the next idea Borges brings: the Man of the Book. This is a much more subtle, and much more plausible, belief
F10.claim: the room contrasted with the Man of the Book, a subtler and more plausible belief

F11.quote: In conclusion: the Crimson Hexagon is the enticing, but impossible goal, that zealots uses as a hollow drive and justification for their destruction.
F11.claim: the room as the enticing but impossible goal, the zealots' hollow drive and justification
F11.lineage: the room as wish and goal

F12.quote: "The Library of Babel" (Spanish: La biblioteca de Babel) is a short story by Argentine author and librarian Jorge Luis Borges (1899–1986), conceiving of a universe in the form of a vast library containing all possible 410-page books of a certain format and character set.
F12.claim: the story: Borges's short story of a universe as a library of all possible 410-page books

F13.quote: The story was originally published in Spanish in Borges' 1941 collection of stories El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan (The Garden of Forking Paths).
F13.claim: first published 1941, in El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan

F14.quote: Two English-language translations appeared approximately simultaneously in 1962, one by James E. Irby in a diverse collection of Borges's works titled Labyrinths and the other by Anthony Kerrigan as part of a collaborative translation of the entirety of Ficciones.
F14.claim: two English translations, 1962: Irby (Labyrinths) and Kerrigan (Ficciones)

F15.quote: Borges' narrator describes how his universe consists of an enormous expanse of adjacent hexagonal rooms.
F15.claim: the narrator's universe: adjacent hexagonal rooms

F16.quote: the inhabitants believe that the books contain every possible ordering of just 25 basic characters (22 letters, the period, the comma, and space)
F16.claim: the books contain every ordering of 25 characters

F17.quote: In the 1941 first edition, five walls of each hexagonal room were lined with bookshelves, while the 1956 edition reduced this to four walls, leaving two sides open.
F17.claim: the architecture revised: five walls of shelves in 1941, four in 1956

F18.quote: This leads to many superstitions, cults, and heresies within the wider organized religion of the library; the "Purifiers" arbitrarily destroy books they deem nonsense as they scour through the library seeking the "Crimson Hexagon" and its illustrated, magical books.
F18.claim: the Purifiers destroy books while seeking the Crimson Hexagon and its illustrated, magical books; one of the library's superstitions
F18.lineage: the room in the Purifiers passage

F19.quote: Others believe that since all books exist in the library, somewhere one of the books must be a perfect index of the library's contents; some even believe that a messianic figure known as the "Man of the Book" has read it, and they travel through the library seeking him.
F19.claim: the perfect index and the Man of the Book, a separate belief

F20.quote: The narrator notes the population of the library has been gravely decimated by centuries of religious conflict and disease, but maintains his faith in the beauty and organization of the library as undeniable proof of a God or other demiurge
F20.claim: the narrator's faith in the library's organization

F21.quote: The story repeats the theme of Borges' 1939 essay "The Total Library" ("La Biblioteca Total"), which in turn acknowledges the earlier development of this theme by Kurd Lasswitz in his 1901 story "The Universal Library" ("Die Universalbibliothek"):

F22.quote: Many of Borges' signature motifs are featured in the story, including infinity, reality, cabalistic reasoning, and labyrinths.
F22.claim: motifs: infinity, reality, cabalistic reasoning, labyrinths

F23.quote: The Library of Babel, a website created by Jonathan Basile, emulates an English-language version of Borges' library.

F24.quote: This article includes a list of general references but lacks sufficient corresponding inline citations.
F24.claim: the article's own limit: insufficient inline citations
